Name: Odissi
Description / Significance: One of India's eight recognized classical dance forms, rooted in temple ritual dance traditions and revived in its modern form largely through the efforts of gurus like Kelucharan Mohapatra in the 20th century.

Name: Gotipua
Description / Significance: The tradition of young boys dressed as female dancers performing devotional dance, historically the form from which many Odissi movements and postures were later drawn.

Name: Chhau
Description / Significance: A martial dance-drama tradition performed without masks (unlike the Purulia or Seraikella styles), rooted in combat training and folk theatre.

Name: Pattachitra
Description / Significance: Cloth-based scroll painting using natural pigments, traditionally depicting Jagannath and Krishna mythology, practiced hereditarily by artist families especially in Raghurajpur village.

Name: Tala Patra Chitra
Description / Significance: The art of engraving illustrations onto dried palm leaves using a stylus, an ancient technique also historically used for manuscript preservation before paper became common.

Name: Pipili Applique Work
Description / Significance: A GI-tagged textile craft originating in the 12th century, traditionally used to make temple umbrellas, canopies, and ceremonial decorations for Jagannath rituals.

Name: Tarakasi (Silver Filigree)
Description / Significance: A GI-tagged craft over 500 years old, involving intricate designs made from thin silver wire, giving Cuttack its nickname as the "Silver City" of Odisha.

Name: Sambalpuri Ikat (Bandha) Weaving
Description / Significance: A GI-tagged tie-dye handloom technique where yarn is dyed in patterns before weaving, producing the distinctive blurred-edge designs seen in Sambalpuri sarees.

Name: Stone Carving
Description / Significance: A craft tradition directly descended from the artisans who built Odisha's medieval temples, now producing decorative items like miniature temple replicas and figures such as Alasa Kanya.

Name: Wood Carving
Description / Significance: Distinguished from other Indian wood-carving traditions by its plain, polished finish without paint or lacquer coating.

Name: Brass and Bell-Metal Work
Description / Significance: Traditionally practiced by the Kansari artisan community, producing household utensils and decorative items through hereditary metalworking skill.

Name: Dhokra Metal Casting
Description / Significance: An ancient lost-wax metal casting technique practiced by tribal artisans, producing figurines and objects with a distinctive rustic, textured surface.

Name: Horn Craft
Description / Significance: Artisans shape polished cattle horn into combs, vases, and figurines like cranes and scorpions, valued for the material's naturally dark, glossy sheen.

Name: Lacquer Work
Description / Significance: A tribal craft practiced mainly by women, used to produce colorful bangles, toys, and decorative household items.

Name: Papier Mâché Craft
Description / Significance: Decorative and festive items made from pulp paper, valued for being both traditional and relatively eco-friendly compared to other craft materials.

Name: Terracotta and Pottery
Description / Significance: An earthenware tradition connecting Odisha's craft culture to its agrarian and natural-material roots.

Name: Zari Embroidery
Description / Significance: Needlework using fine gold and silver threads to add richness to fabrics used in both everyday and ceremonial clothing.

Name: Ganjifa
Description / Significance: Traditional hand-painted circular playing cards, a craft that has become rare nationally, with only a small number of practicing artisan families remaining.

Name: Kapdaganda Shawl
Description / Significance: A GI-tagged shawl handwoven by Dongria Kondh women of the Niyamgiri hills, featuring geometric embroidery symbolizing trees and mountains central to the community's identity and their resistance to bauxite mining on their sacred hills.

Name: Sambalpuri Saree Weaving
Description / Significance: The broader handloom tradition behind Sambalpuri textiles, historically produced by weaving communities in and around Sambalpur district.

Name: Danda Nata
Description / Significance: A ritual folk dance-drama performed during the month of Chaitra, combining physical endurance rituals with dramatic storytelling.

Name: Dalkhai
Description / Significance: A vibrant tribal folk dance of western Odisha, traditionally performed by women during festivals like Nuakhai and Bhai Jiuntia.

Name: Ghumura
Description / Significance: A ritual war-dance tradition from Kalahandi, performed with a distinctive drum of the same name, historically associated with martial preparation and later folk celebration.

Name: Dhemsa
Description / Significance: A community folk dance form of western and southern Odisha's tribal communities, typically performed in large circles during festivals.

Name: Chang
Description / Significance: A traditional folk musical and dance form of western Odisha, named after the large drum central to its performance.

Name: Rock Shelter Paintings
Description / Significance: Early historic-period paintings dated to roughly 300 BCE–100 CE, found at sites including Vikramkhol and Sitabhinji, among the oldest surviving pictorial art in the region.

Name: Odissi Classical Music
Description / Significance: A distinct classical vocal and instrumental music tradition with its own repertoire, historically performed alongside Odissi dance in temple contexts.

Name: Jhoomar
Description / Significance: A folk dance performed during the harvest season, marking agricultural celebration through communal movement and song.

Name: Shola Pith Craft
Description / Significance: Delicate decorative work carved from the pith of the shola plant, traditionally used to create ornamentation for deity idols and ceremonial items.

Name: Sand Art of Puri
Description / Significance:
A modern but internationally recognized living tradition of sculpting large-scale art directly on Puri's beach, most associated globally with artist Sudarsan Pattnaik.
